newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Rescue starts for 20 buried in Australian landslide.
newsitem.headline: Rescue starts for 20 buried in Australian landslide.

text.p: Up to 20 people were feared killed or seriously injured after a landslide demolished two lodges overnight at Thredbo, Australia's most popular ski resort, police said on Thursday.

Police said they believed up to 20 people were inside the Carinya and Bimbadeen lodges when the landslide occurred just before midnight on Wednesday at the Thredbo Alpine Village in the Snowy Mountains, 150 km (90 miles) southwest of Canberra.
Rescue operations in the freezing temperatures were delayed more than 10 hours because the site was dangerously unstable and police at the scene said the situation looked grim.
"It looks very dismal," said police chief superintendent Charlie Sanderson, when asked whether there were any survivors.
Eyewitnesses said they initially heard voices from beneath the rubble, but police said no contact had been made.
"I have not heard any reports in the last six hours that there is any voices or any contact being made with the people there," Sanderson said.

Sanderson said police believe one person was in the Carinya lodge when it was crushed by the landslide and sent cascading onto the Bimbadeen lodge, which is believed to have contained 19 people -- mostly resort staff.

Shortly after 10.00 a.m. (2400 GMT), 24 rescue workers began sifting through the rubble by hand, but police said they were awaiting an aerial survey before launching a major rescue operation because the site was so unstable.
Heat-imaging equipment was being brought in to search for survivors.
Eyewitnesses said the landslide sounded like a big gust of wind that shook the lodges perched on the side of the mountain.
"We just heard this enormous rush like I'd imagine you'd experience with a tornado just hitting a building...," said Glenn Milne, who was holidaying in an adjacent lodge.
Police at first feared up to 100 people were trapped.
Milne, one of the first at the scene, said he heard voices crying from the rubble as tourists tried to find survivors before police halted rescue efforts over safety concerns.
"We heard three voices, three separate voices. We got down into the rubble and we started clawing away chunks of rubble," said Milne, a television reporter.
"When the lodges collapsed, cars also came down on top -- they were teetering on the edge of the rubble. Every time we moved chunks of rubble, the cars were unstable at the top."
The landslide occurred just before midnight at a time when Thredbo, at an altitude of 1,370 metres (4,494 feet), was packed with thousands of Australian and foreign visitors.
Thredbo sits on a ridge facing the snow-covered mountain range of the Kosciuszko National Park, which rises to 2,037 metres (6,683 feet).
Australia's ski season runs from June to October, but a poor start to the season has seen little snow fall on the village.
Police believe seepage from a mountain spring may have caused the earth to give way, sending tonnes of dirt, rock and gum trees crashing onto the lodges.
"It looks like someone has taken a great big bulldozer and just drove over both the lodges and they just slid down the hill," one unidentified witness told reporters.

"There is really nothing left of them but bits and pieces. It reminds me of looking at a picture of a tornado site or something where it's just cleaned a path through and on either side there is no damage whatsoever," he said.
